analytic.title: Deferrable Scheduling for Temporal Consistency: Schedulability Analysis and Overhead Reduction

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The deferrable scheduling algorithm for fixed priority transactions is demonstrated to be a very effective approach for minimizing real-time update transaction workload while maintaining temporal validity of real-time data. This paper examines the schedulability of deferrable scheduling and presents a sufficient condition. While its on-line scheduling overhead is a concern, we propose a hyperperiod based DS-FP approach satisfying the temporal validity constraint with low overhead. The algorithm, namely DEferrable Scheduling with Hyperperiod by Schedule Adjustment (DESH-SA), adjusts the DS-FP schedule in an interval so that the adjusted schedule in the interval can be repeated infinitely. Our experiments demonstrate that DESH-SA can reduce scheduling overhead of DS-FP and also achieve update workload near optimal.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Many real-time embedded systems such as airplanes, robots, and industry process control systems, are heavily dependent on real-time data sampled from real world entities in the external environment. Those data values, which are sampled by sensors, become invalid with the passage of time as their real world values continually change. The sampled data are stored in Real-Time Data Base Systems (RTDBSs). In this manner, data producers are separated from data consumers, which may read data from RTDBSs. The sensor update transactions constantly sample real world data and write them into RTDBSs whose applications control the activities of actuators, as shown in Figure 1.

One way to define the data correctness in RTDBSs is the validity interval. It stipulates that at any time, values of realtime data in RTDBSs must always be valid in order to keep track of environmental changes and respond to the changes timely. This has been known as validity constraint [17,23] or age constraint [2]. In practice, many real-time applications for process control require continuous sensor data update regardless of how much a data value itself changes, i.e., the validity constraint must be strictly enforced. div.head: Wireless Sensor Network
div.p: Figure 1. A RTDBS control system connecting to wireless sensor network loop control algorithm must be periodically executed many times during deadtime, which is a time interval between requested actuator action and its effect detected by sensors. To satisfy the validity constraint, it is necessary to produce a schedule of sensor update transactions for all real-time data so that for any consecutive updates of a real-time data object, the next update can be completed before the previous data version expires. Application transactions may be triggered due to environmental changes committed by sensor update transactions. Such application transactions, namely triggered transactions, may invoke actuators to respond to such changes timely.

Minimizing sensor workload has been an important design issue in the past studies [12,22,23] because (1) it reduces sensor energy consumption; (2) it may allow a RT-DBS to accommodate more sensor update transactions; and (3) it leaves more processor capacity of the RTDBS to other workload, e.g., triggered transactions. The commonly used approach is to model update transactions as periodic tasks in which the update time is the task execution time. In the Half-Half (HH) scheme, the task period is defined as half of the validity interval. It is known that if the HH task set is schedulable, the validity constraint is satisfied. HH scheme has the upper bound on CPU utilization; there is no need to schedule transactions more frequently to meet the validity constraint. The question now becomes if less sensor update workload can be achieved. [22] formally defines a scheme, namely More-Less (ML), which guarantees the validity con-1 straint yet utilizes less CPU. ML finds the worst-case response time of a periodic transaction, and if it is less than half of the validity interval, ML sets it as relative deadline of the transaction while the difference of the validity interval and the relative deadline as its period. Compared to HH, ML increases transaction period accordingly. Increased period means reduced sensor update workload. Lately, [23] proposed the DS-FP algorithm to schedule sensor update transactions adaptively. The idea of DS-FP is to schedule a sensor transaction job as late as possible and use its response time as the job's relative deadline, which is usually less than the worst-case response time of its transaction. Its experimental studies demonstrate that DS-FP outperforms HH and ML significantly.

However, [23] left many questions unanswered. This paper aims at answering some of the open questions either theoretically or experimentally. Specifically, Section 3 theoretically demonstrates that DS-FP is better than ML in terms of schedulability after a brief review of related work in Section 2. The drawback of DS-FP is its time complexity for on-line scheduling [23]. The varying overhead for computing part of the DS-FP schedule each time in DS-FP also results in unpredictability for on-line scheduling in realtime systems. This paper thus aims at reducing the on-line scheduling overhead of the DS-FP algorithm. In particular, Section 4 proposes a DS-FP based algorithm, namely DEferrable Scheduling with Hyperperiod based on Schedule Adjustment (DESH-SA) that creates hyperperiod from the DS-FP schedule. The sensor transaction set can be scheduled while the validity constraint can be guaranteed by repeating the schedule in the hyperperiod. In this manner, the on-line scheduling complexity is reduced to constant, i.e., . The algorithm is experimentally studied in Section 5 and Section 6 concludes the paper.

div.head: Background and Related Work
div.p: This section briefly reviews temporal validity of realtime data, the More-Less (ML) [2,22] and deferrable scheduling (DS-FP) [23] algorithms. Formal definitions of the frequently used symbols are given in Table 1.

To monitor the states of entities faithfully, real-time data must be refreshed by sensor update transactions before they become invalid. The actual length of the temporal validity interval of a real-time data object is application dependent [17,18,16]. One of the important design goals of RTDBSs is to guarantee that real-time data remain fresh, i.e., they are always valid. Definition 2.1: A real-time data object ( ) at time is temporally valid (or temporally consistent) if, for its update finished last before , the sampling time (r ) plus the validity interval ( ) of the data object is not less than , i.e., r [17].

A data value for real-time data object sampled at any time will be valid up to . We assume that the network delay for an sensor transaction job to be sent from a sensor to the RTDBS (i.e., jitter between sampling time at the sensor and release time at the RTDBS) is zero for convenience of presentation. Our results can be easily extended to the case that jitter is non-zero if the maximum jitter of a transaction is known. In the presence of non-zero jitters, we can transform a transaction (with validity length and maximum jitter ) to a transaction (with validity length and zero jitter). Such a transformation guarantees that if can meet its validity constraint, then can also meet its validity constraint. Readers are also referred to [22] for how jitters are handled in ML. Thus, we assume zero jitters in the rest of this paper. Given a set of transactions , we also assume that has higher priority than for . Recently, there has been extensive work in RTDBSs for guaranteeing the validity constraint (or similarityconstraint) of real-time data [19,10,11,12,5,21,9,13,6,7,3,22,23]. The deferrable scheduling algorithm is proposed in [23]. ML is studied in [22,13,3], which reduces update workload compared to the Half-Half approach [17,12] while guaranteeing the validity constraint. Compared to ML, DS-FP reduces update workload further by adaptively adjusting the separation of two consecutive jobs while satisfying the validity constraint.

The EDL algorithm proposed in [4] processes tasks as late as possible based on the Earliest Deadline algorithm [15]. EDL assumes that all deadlines of tasks are given whereas DS-FP and DESH-SA algorithms derive deadlines dynamically. The validity constrained scheduling, e.g., ML, DS-FP, and DESH-SA algorithms, are different from the distance constrained scheduling, which guarantees a bound of the finishing times of two consecutive instances of a task [8]. div.head: DEferrable Scheduling with Hyperperiod: Schedule Adjustment (DESH-SA)
div.p: The DS-FP algorithm is very effective on reducing processor utilization while guaranteeing the validity constraint.

However, its on-line scheduling overhead in terms of time complexity is much higher than that of ML. Moreover, the scheduling overhead of DS-FP depends on the number of transactions and validity length of updated data [23]. Thus, DS-FP can become very expensive, e.g., when the transaction set becomes large. In this section, we present DEferrable Scheduling with Hyperperiod based on Schedule Adjustment (DESH-SA), a DS-FP based algorithm that can reduce on-line scheduling overhead while achieving processor utilization close to that of DS-FP. By schedule adjustment, we mean changing release times and deadlines of jobs. The basic idea of DESH-SA is to construct a hyperperiod schedule off-line for , a set of validity constrained transactions. Suppose the first hyperperiod of the schedule has length . If the first hyperperiod of can be constructed by adjusting the DS-FP schedule in time interval , the complete schedule can be constructed by repeating the first hyperperiod of infinitely for every time units. Thus, the DESH-SA algorithm consists of two parts: an algorithm for constructing the hyperperiod off-line (see Alg. 4.1 for DESH-SA hyperperiod construction) and an algorithm for scheduling transactions on-line. The latter is trivial once a hyperperiod is constructed because it only needs to repeat the hyperperiod schedule. div.head: Conclusions
div.p: This paper sheds light on the theory of deferrable scheduling by presenting a sufficient condition for its schedulability. Moreover, it presents a novel and practical approach derived from DS-FP, namely DESH-SA, which reduces on-line scheduling overhead of DS-FP to . Our experiments demonstrate that DESH-SA is a very effective approach for minimizing sensor update workload while guaranteeing the validity constraint, and it is efficient in terms of time and space complexity.

div.head: Performance Evaluation
div.p: In this section, we conducted experiments to study the performance of the DESH-SA algorithm. In the experiments, we demonstrate whether DESH-SA can find a hyperperiod, and if so, how much extra CPU workload it may incur compared to DS-FP. The hyperperiod length of DESH-SA is also demonstrated to study its space efficiency.

div.head: Simulation Model and Parameters
div.p: For simplicity of simulation study, only one version of a real-time data object is maintained. Upon refreshing a real-time data object, the older version is discarded. We ignore the on-line scheduling overhead in our experiments, and consider it to be for all algorithms (which is true for DESH-SA algorithm). This is in favor of DS-FP as its scheduling overhead is ignored in our experimental results for CPU workload. The primary performance metric used in the experiments is the CPU workload resulting from sensor update transactions.

A summary of the parameters and default settings used in experiments are presented in . CPU workload comparison for the parameters follow those used in [22], which are originally from air traffic control applications. Two categories of parameters are defined: system and update transaction parameters. For system configurations, we only consider a single CPU, main memory based RTDBS. The number of real-time data is varied from 50 to 300 and the validity length of each real-time data object is uniformly varied from 4000 to 8000 ms. For update transactions, it is assumed that each transaction updates one real-time data object, and its CPU time is uniformly varied from 5 to 15 ms.

div.head: Experimental Results
div.p: In this subsection, the CPU workloads of sensor update transactions produced by DS-FP and DESH-SA are quantitatively compared. In the experiments, update transactions are generated randomly according to the parameter settings in Table 2. In DESH-SA algorithm, transaction with maximum validity interval is run at least 200 jobs so that the CPU workload of the first hyperperiod is close to . Then the idle times following the completion of those jobs under DS-FP are chosen as candidates. Those candidates are tested to find out whether the interval can be used as the first hyperperiod.
